item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by nature has strong lust, and he constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of lust. By nature he has strong ill-will, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of ill-will. By nature he has strong delusion, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of delusion. With pain and grief, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life that is fully complete and pure. At the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in this realm. This, monks, is called a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence.…
item.description:
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on impermanence, what is called the conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 62 – Mahārāhulovādasutta

item.title: Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā: Nandā, look at this body — Diseased, impure, stinking. Develop the mind on foulness, One-pointed, well-concentrated. As this body, so that…
item.description:
Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā:

Nandā, look at this body —
Diseased, impure, stinking.
Develop the mind on foulness,
One-pointed, well-concentrated.

As this body, so that body —
As that body, so this body —
Foul, rotting —
Only fools delight in it.

Thus contemplate this body,
Day and night without fatigue.
With your own wisdom,
Therefore escape.
With your own wisdom,
Escape pride in beauty,
And see truly
What fools see.

This city is built of bones,
Plastered with flesh and blood.
Within dwell aging and death,
Conceit and hypocrisy.

Without heedlessness,
Rightly contemplate that body —
The true nature of this body
Is seen inside and out.
I am disenchanted with the body,
My mind is dispassionate.
Without heedlessness, free from bonds,
I am at peace, stilled.

From: Therīgāthā 5.4

item.title: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
item.description:
“Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then because he delights, praises, and dwells with lust, delight arises. With the arising of delight, lust arises. With the arising of lust, bondage arises. Bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Even if he lives in remote lodgings, in forests, in groves, in quiet places, with little sound, little noise, free from people’s breath, secluded, suitable for seclusion — still he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Why? Because craving, the companion, has not been abandoned by him. Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.63

item.title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and…
item.description:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and humans delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, devas and humans dwell in suffering.

Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

The wise are open-eyed,
Like light clearly shining,
The foolish, even though near,
Do not understand the Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.136

item.title: O monks, these six sense bases — Where they are unrestrained, There suffering comes to be. Those who learn to guard them, To restrain and…
item.description:
O monks, these six sense bases —
Where they are unrestrained,
There suffering comes to be.
Those who learn to guard them,
To restrain and protect them,
With faith as their companion,
Dwell freed from sensual lust.

Seeing forms that are pleasing,
Seeing forms that are displeasing,
Restrain the path of lust
For forms that are pleasing —
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in forms.’

Having heard sounds —
Pleasing and displeasing,
Do not be infatuated with pleasing sounds.
Restrain the mind’s aversion
For sounds that are displeasing,
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in sounds.’

Having smelled fragrant, delightful odors,
Having smelled foul, loathsome odors —
Restrain aversion for loathsome odors,
And for delightful ones,
Do not let desire dominate.

Having tasted sweet flavors,
And also flavors that are not sweet,
Do not develop greed
When enjoying a sweet taste,
Do not utter words of opposition
When tasting what is not sweet.

When touched by pleasant contact,
Do not be infatuated with lust;
When touched by painful contact,
Do not be violently shaken.
For both contacts — pleasant and painful —
Remain equanimous,
Without approval or opposition,
Whatever contact may arise.

Those who follow proliferated perceptions,
Who are lost in conceptual proliferation,
Who act upon false thoughts —
Abandon all household activities
Born of the mind,
Practice restraint in your actions,
Directing yourself to the path of seclusion.

Thus, with the mind well-developed
Regarding these six sense bases,
Whatever contact occurs,
The mind is not disturbed.
Having subdued both greed and hatred,
O monk, go to the far shore,
Beyond the bonds of birth and death.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94

item.title: “He contemplates all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as…
item.description:
“He contemplates all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. He turns his mind away from these states and directs it towards the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ If he is firm in this, he attains the destruction of the defilements. If he does not yet attain the destruction of the defilements, then by that same Dhamma-lust, Dhamma-delight, and by the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is reborn spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes) and there attains final Nibbāna, never to return from that world.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 64 – Mahāmāluṅkyasutta

item.title: “What are the five mental shackles not yet cut off? Monks, here a monk is not free from lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, craving for…
item.description:
“What are the five mental shackles not yet cut off? Monks, here a monk is not free from lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, craving for sensual pleasures. Monks, for a monk who is not free from lust … craving for sensual pleasures, his mind does not incline to exertion, commitment, persistence, striving. If one’s mind does not incline to exertion, commitment, persistence, striving, this is the first mental shackle not yet cut off.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 16 – Cetokhilasutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk one who sees sensual pleasures? When sensual pleasures are seen, then desire, lust for sensual pleasure, infatuation with sensual…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk one who sees sensual pleasures? When sensual pleasures are seen, then desire, lust for sensual pleasure, infatuation with sensual pleasure, and fever of sensual pleasure have no underlying tendency regarding sensual pleasures. Suppose, monks, there is a pit of glowing embers deeper than a man’s height, filled with glowing embers that are neither flaming nor smoking. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. Two strong men grab him by both arms and drag him toward that pit. He twists his body this way and that. Why? Because he knows: ‘I will fall into this pit of embers. Because of this, I will meet death or deadly suffering.’ So too, monks, a monk sees sensual pleasures as a pit of embers. And one who sees sensual pleasures thus has no desire, lust, infatuation, or fever for sensual pleasures as an underlying tendency.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244

item.title: “Carpenter, what are wholesome thoughts? Renunciation thought, non-ill-will thought, harmlessness thought. These, Carpenter, are called wholesome thoughts.”
item.description:
“Carpenter, what are wholesome thoughts? Renunciation thought, non-ill-will thought, harmlessness thought. These, Carpenter, are called wholesome thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 78 – Samaṇamuṇḍikasutta
